# Chapter 1: A small garden

A gardener checks the soil before adding water. Dry leaves can have more than one cause.

The gardener suggests keeping a short record, rather than assuming that every plant needs the same schedule.

# Chapter 2: Feedback

An action can change the conditions that guide the next action. In this example, the gardener measures moisture after watering.

This observation may help adjust tomorrow's watering, but one measurement does not establish a universal rule.

# Chapter 3: Delay

Some changes take time to become visible. Adding more water immediately can hide the effect of the earlier watering.

# Chapter 4: Boundaries

The garden shares sunlight and water with its surroundings. Choosing a boundary helps a reader describe the example, but does not remove those connections.

# Chapter 5: Records

A record is useful when its entries describe comparable observations. Missing entries should remain visible.

# Chapter 6: Variation

Plants can differ. The author proposes looking at those differences before copying a successful routine.

# Chapter 7: Limits

An example illustrates an idea. It does not by itself prove that the idea applies to every situation.

# Chapter 8: Review

The gardener revisits earlier notes and changes the plan when observations disagree with expectations.
